passage: The hostel common room smelled of instant coffee when Mehak put her phone face down on the table. Sonali looked up from her lab record. "Your papa again?" Mehak nodded. "I told him I'm taking the design elective next semester instead of the extra accounts paper. He said the firm has carried the family name for three generations and I'm being ungrateful. Then Mummy came on and said college has made me lost." She pressed her thumbs against her eyes. "Maybe I am. I don't even know if I hate accounts or just never chose them." Sonali pushed her own mug across the table. "So find out. Take the elective and see how it feels." Mehak drew two columns in the margin of her notebook, one headed Mine? and the other Handed to me. Both stayed half empty until lights-out.

qa.q: What did Mehak tell her papa she was taking next semester?
qa.a: She told him she was taking the design elective instead of the extra accounts paper.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she pressed her thumbs against her eyes?
qa.a: She felt guilty and hurt at being called ungrateful and lost, and also unsure, because she admits she doesn't know if she hates accounts or just never chose them.

qa.q: When Mehak drew the two columns, what choice was she making, and how could she use it?
qa.a: She chose to sort honestly what was hers from what was handed to her, instead of simply obeying or rebelling. Trying the elective would give her real answers for the Mine? column.

qa.q: How might Mehak's papa see the elective differently from Mehak?
qa.a: To him the firm carries three generations of family name, so a change can feel like turning away from the family; to Mehak it is a way to find out what she actually likes.

grounding: A young adult who questions the family career is called ungrateful and lost, and feels guilt while trying to sort what is truly hers from what was inherited.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
Dear Sunaina didi,
You're the only one in the family I can write this to without the whole group chat finding out. I didn't sit for the prelims this year. I told Papa at Diwali, and Chacha said, loud enough for everyone, "Three generations of officers and this girl is lost." Papa didn't defend me. Later he said I was being ungrateful after all those coaching fees.
I keep replaying it at night here in my room in Pune. I do feel guilty. The fees were real. But I've started asking which parts of the plan were ever mine. Wanting to work with people and be useful, I think that's mine. The exact exam, the exact uniform, I'm not sure.
Is it wrong to take a year to find out? You left engineering once. Did anyone talk to you for a while after?
Love,
Nandini

qa.q: Where is Nandini while she writes this letter?
qa.a: She is in her room in Pune.

qa.q: Why does Nandini feel guilty even while she questions the plan?
qa.a: She knows the coaching fees were real, so stepping away feels like wasting what her family gave, even though she's not sure the exam path was ever hers.

qa.q: What choice is Nandini weighing when she asks about taking a year, and what could guide it?
qa.a: She is choosing between going back to the inherited exam path and taking time to test what she wants. Starting from the part she's sure of, working with people, could guide what she tries.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina understand Nandini better than the rest of the family?
qa.a: Sunaina once left engineering too, so she may know how it feels to be called lost and how lonely the silence afterwards can be.

grounding: A young adult who steps off the family's exam path is called lost and ungrateful, feels guilty and alone, and asks which parts of the plan were ever hers.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: You asked why I went quiet at the wedding, Kamal. Okay. My family has run the sweet shop in the old market for four generations, and everyone assumes I'll take the counter after Dadaji. At the wedding my Bua asked when I'm starting. I said I'm not sure I want to. Just that. And she said, "Such an ungrateful girl, Arohi. That shop fed you." After that my cousins kept forgetting to call me for photos. I laughed it off, but on the drive home I felt like the only person in the car. Here's what I can't explain to them. I love the shop. The smell of ghee at six in the morning, Dadaji's hands folding the boxes. I just don't know if I love it the way you love something you chose, or the way you love the wallpaper you grew up with. I want time to find out without being treated like a traitor.

qa.q: How long has Arohi's family run the sweet shop?
qa.a: For four generations, in the old market.

qa.q: What does Arohi feel unsure about when comparing the shop to the wallpaper she grew up with?
qa.a: She's unsure whether her love for the shop is truly her own choice or only familiarity, and not knowing leaves her confused and lonely.

qa.q: What choice does Arohi face after her Bua's comment, and what could help her?
qa.a: She can give in to avoid being seen as a traitor, or ask for time to test whether the shop is really hers. Talking it through with a friend like Kamal is a first honest step.

qa.q: How might Arohi's Bua see Arohi's hesitation?
qa.a: In her eyes the shop fed Arohi, so hesitating to take it over looks like ingratitude rather than an honest question.

grounding: A young adult who is unsure about taking over the family shop is called ungrateful, feels left out, and wants time to learn what is truly hers.

passage: After the branch shutters came down, Jahnavi knocked on Rafiq's cabin with a sheet of paper folded twice. "Sir, can I ask for something small?" Rafiq, her branch manager, waved her in. For three years she had followed exactly the plan her parents made the day she cleared the bank exam: counter, loans desk, promotion test. Last month, while training two new joiners, she had noticed she stayed late without once looking at the clock. "I'd like to run the induction sessions for new staff, alongside my desk work. Maybe for three months, to see if I'm any good." Rafiq read her plan. "And your parents?" "I told them on Sunday. I said the job they pushed me toward gave me steady ground, and I'm grateful. I'm not quitting. I just want to see what I'd build on it." He signed the sheet. "Three months, then."

qa.q: How long had Jahnavi followed her parents' plan at the bank?
qa.a: For three years: counter, loans desk, promotion test.

qa.q: What did staying late without looking at the clock make Jahnavi think?
qa.a: It made her think she might truly enjoy training people, something she noticed for herself rather than something planned for her.

qa.q: Why was asking for a three-month trial a wise choice for Jahnavi?
qa.a: It let her test a small change without throwing away the steady job she still values, so she gets real evidence instead of a dramatic break.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's parents have felt hearing her Sunday explanation?
qa.a: They may have felt respected and relieved, since she thanked them for the steady ground and said she wasn't quitting, so the change didn't sound like a rejection.

grounding: A young professional who sees she followed her parents' script tests a small change, keeps what she values and explains it to them with respect.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
Dear Vijay bhaiya,
You'll hear from Papa soon, so I wanted you to hear it from me first. I'm not applying for the master's abroad this year.
Don't panic. I'm not leaving engineering. I still love the puzzle of code, and that part is mine, not only the dream of a father who calls me his engineer daughter. What I've realised is that I picked every step because it was the next box on his list, and I never asked what I wanted to build.
So I'm trying something small. From next month I'm moving to the team that makes attendance software for village schools. Same company, same pay. If I hate it in six months, I'll know.
I'll tell Papa on the Sunday call. I want to thank him properly first, because his push got me here, and then explain. Could you be on the call? Not to fight for me. Just so I'm not alone.
Preeti

qa.q: Which team is Preeti moving to from next month?
qa.a: The team that makes attendance software for village schools, in the same company.

qa.q: Why does Preeti want Vijay on the Sunday call?
qa.a: She feels nervous about telling Papa and wants company so she isn't alone, though she doesn't want Vijay to fight for her.

qa.q: What makes Preeti's plan a careful choice rather than a dramatic break?
qa.a: She keeps the coding she truly loves, stays in the same company and gives the new team six months, so she can learn without burning anything down.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if Preeti starts the call by thanking him?
qa.a: He may feel his effort is being honoured rather than rejected, which could make him readier to listen to her new plan.

grounding: A young professional who realises she ticked off her father's list keeps the parts she endorses, tries one small change and plans to explain it with respect.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: Nilesh, you said the theme of your podcast this month is plans that changed. Mine didn't really change. It got edited. My life was written before I could read: the good daughter, Gurleen, will teach at Nanaji's school, marry by twenty-five, live two streets away. And I did it. I topped my B.Ed class and was back at that school by twenty-two. Then last year a Class 8 girl asked me what I had wanted to be, and I had no answer. That scared me more than any fight could. I didn't quit, and I didn't shout at my parents. I kept teaching, because the classroom turns out to be truly mine. But I asked for one year before any wedding talk, and I started a free evening reading club in our mohalla that nobody planned for me. When I explained it to Mummy, I said, "You gave me the ground. Let me choose some of what grows on it."

qa.q: What did the Class 8 girl ask Gurleen?
qa.a: She asked Gurleen what she had wanted to be.

qa.q: Why did the girl's question scare Gurleen more than a fight could?
qa.a: Having no answer made Gurleen feel she had lived a script written for her without ever choosing it herself.

qa.q: Which choices show Gurleen changing course without burning everything down?
qa.a: She kept teaching because it is truly hers, asked for one year before wedding talk and started the evening reading club, testing small changes instead of quitting.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's Mummy hear the line about the ground and what grows on it?
qa.a: She may hear respect for what the family gave rather than rejection, which makes it easier to accept Gurleen's own choices.

grounding: A young teacher who notices her life followed a family script keeps the teaching she endorses, makes small new choices and explains them respectfully.

passage:
"Nani, Nani!" Zeenat toddled in holding a wooden duck.
"What have you got, jaan?" asked Tanuja Nani.
"Duck! Look!" Zeenat pushed it into her lap.
"Such a fine duck!"
Zeenat held half her biscuit to Nani's mouth. "You eat."
"For me? Thank you, my love."
Then Zeenat bumped her head on the table leg, wailed and reached up both arms. Nani lifted her and rocked. Soon Zeenat wriggled down and went back to the duck.

qa.q: What toy did Zeenat show Tanuja Nani?
qa.a: A wooden duck.

qa.q: What does Zeenat reaching up both arms after bumping her head suggest she expects?
qa.a: She expects Nani to pick her up and comfort her, because she trusts Nani to be there.

qa.q: Which moment shows Nani's comfort working, and what could Nani keep doing?
qa.a: After Nani rocked her, Zeenat soon wriggled down and went back to the duck. Nani can keep giving quick, warm comfort so Zeenat feels safe to play again.

qa.q: What is it like for Tanuja Nani when Zeenat holds half the biscuit to her mouth?
qa.a: It is likely touching for Nani, a small gift of trust and love from the toddler ❤️

grounding: A reliably comforted toddler shows a toy, shares food and seeks a hug from a trusted grandmother, then goes back to play.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday. Arnab (2 years). Written by Gopika.
Arrived teary and came straight to me for a long hug. At snack time he pushed an apple slice into my hand. Twice he brought me the red truck just to show it, waited for my "Wow!" and ran back. Woke from nap upset and settled quickly on my lap.
Next: I'll keep greeting him at the gate this week and tell his mother how quickly he settles now 🙂

qa.q: What did Arnab bring Gopika twice?
qa.a: The red truck, just to show it.

qa.q: Why do you think Arnab waited for Gopika's "Wow!" before running back?
qa.a: He wanted Gopika to share his excitement, and the reply made him feel safe and confident enough to go back and play.

qa.q: What is wise about Gopika's plan to greet Arnab at the gate?
qa.a: Being the same warm person every morning keeps his comfort reliable, which is what lets him settle and explore.

qa.q: How might Arnab's mother feel reading that he settles quickly now?
qa.a: She would probably feel relieved that he trusts his caregiver and manages well away from home.

grounding: A toddler who trusts his caregiver hugs Gopika, shares his apple and shows off his toy, building early closeness.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house, Sonali was sorting wheat when little Mehak, not yet two, waddled over with a fistful of puffed rice. She pushed a few grains into her mother's mouth and laughed. A goat bleated at the gate. Mehak froze, then ran to bury her face in Sonali's dupatta. Sonali stroked her back and hummed. Soon Mehak peeked out, fetched her clay whistle and held it up high for her mother to see.

qa.q: What did Mehak push into her mother's mouth?
qa.a: A few grains of puffed rice.

qa.q: What does Mehak burying her face in Sonali's dupatta suggest she feels?
qa.a: The goat startled her, and she ran to her mother because she feels safe with her and trusts her to comfort her.

qa.q: Which of Sonali's choices helped Mehak go back to playing?
qa.a: Sonali stayed calm, stroked her back and hummed instead of hurrying her, so Mehak felt safe enough to peek out and fetch her whistle.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel when Mehak holds up the clay whistle for her?
qa.a: She would likely feel warm and proud that her daughter wants to share her small treasures with her.

grounding: A toddler who is reliably comforted shares food, runs to her mother when scared and then shows her a toy.

passage: Beta, you want to know about best friends? When I was ten, in our lane in Lucknow, Naveen was mine. Only mine. People called me Farhan the shadow. We shared one bicycle, one tiffin and every secret. I told him I was scared of the dark and still slept holding Ammi's dupatta. He swore on his cricket bat he'd never tell. Two weeks later, in front of the whole class, he said it out loud, and everyone laughed. I went home and wouldn't eat. It felt as if the floor had gone. For a month I sat alone. Then Naveen came to our gate, red in the face, and said sorry. I forgave him slowly. Your Dadi says I still pick friends carefully. But I still pick them.

qa.q: What secret did Farhan tell Naveen?
qa.a: That Farhan was scared of the dark and still slept holding Ammi's dupatta.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel after Naveen told the class?
qa.a: Farhan felt devastated and betrayed, refused to eat at home and felt as if the floor had gone.

qa.q: When Naveen came to the gate, what choice did Farhan face, and what came of it?
qa.a: Farhan could stay shut off or forgive slowly. Forgiving slowly saved the friendship and led to careful trust instead of no trust.

qa.q: Why might Naveen have come to the gate red in the face?
qa.a: He probably felt ashamed of breaking his promise and missed his best friend after a month apart.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood best friend who shared every secret and then betrayed one, leaving deep hurt that slowly healed.

passage: Rain hammered the school bus roof, and the only empty seat was next to Shreya. Manjula stood in the aisle, dripping, clutching her bag. That morning Ruchika had whispered, "Is it true you're moving to a one-room flat?" Only one person knew that. Manjula had told Shreya under the slide last week, pinkie-swear, best friends forever. "Sit down, child, the bus is moving," the conductor called. Manjula sat, pressed against the window. Shreya leaned over. "Manju, I only told Ruchika because she asked why you looked sad..." Manjula turned to the fogged glass. Her throat hurt. She had never told anyone a real secret before Shreya, and now she didn't know if she ever would again.

qa.q: Where had Manjula told Shreya her secret?
qa.a: Under the slide last week, with a pinkie-swear.

qa.q: What does Manjula turning to the fogged glass suggest she feels?
qa.a: She feels deeply hurt and betrayed and can't face Shreya yet; her sore throat shows she is close to tears.

qa.q: What could Manjula do once she's ready, instead of deciding never to share again?
qa.a: She could tell Shreya how much it hurt and hear the explanation, then decide slowly how far to trust again rather than shutting everyone out.

qa.q: How might Shreya be feeling as Manjula turns away?
qa.a: Shreya may feel guilty and panicky, trying to explain and afraid of losing a best friend 😔

grounding: A child whose one best friend passes on her secret feels crushed, showing how much the close friendship meant.

passage: Every evening in their Pune colony, Ramesh and Yamini climbed onto the water-tank ledge, the one place grown-ups never checked. There Ramesh told her things he told nobody: that he was scared of the new maths teacher, that he had cried at the end of a film. Yamini shared her own secrets, and together they drew a map of the colony with their hideouts marked in red. On Monday the science-fair pairs went up on the board. They had promised to be partners. But Yamini's name was next to Pallavi's. She had signed up on Friday without a word. Ramesh walked home the long way, kicking a stone. At dinner he pushed his dal around, and when his mother asked, he said, "Nothing," and went to bed early.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh and Yamini go every evening?
qa.a: They climbed onto the water-tank ledge in their Pune colony.

qa.q: What does Ramesh saying "Nothing" and going to bed early suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels betrayed and too hurt to talk; the broken promise from his closest friend has knocked him flat.

qa.q: What could Ramesh try the next day instead of avoiding Yamini?
qa.a: He could ask her on the ledge why she signed up without telling him and say how it felt, which gives the friendship a chance to mend.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's mother see his quiet evening?
qa.a: She can tell from the pushed-around dal that something is wrong, and may worry and want to help gently without forcing him to talk.

grounding: A child who shares secrets with one best friend is shattered when she breaks their promise, showing the risk and depth of that closeness.

passage: Last year my photo page looked perfect: the debate trophy, the beach trip, the new haircut. I spent twenty minutes on every caption. People left hearts under everything, and I, Yamini, still ate lunch pretending to text so nobody would notice I had nobody to talk to. I was scared that if anyone saw how often I doubted myself, they'd leave. Then in March, Vaibhav from my bus stop asked why a girl with such a perfect page never looked happy in person. I almost said, "I'm fine." Instead I said, "I don't know who I am when I'm not performing." He didn't laugh. He said he felt the same about his gym videos. We talk at the bus stop most mornings now. It's only one person. It's more than all those hearts.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav ask Yamini in March?
qa.a: He asked why a girl with such a perfect page never looked happy in person.

qa.q: Why did Yamini pretend to text at lunch?
qa.a: She was afraid people would notice she had nobody to talk to, and worried that showing her doubts would make them leave.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yamini, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing to say "I don't know who I am when I'm not performing" instead of "I'm fine." One honest answer let a real friendship begin.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have gained from Yamini's honest reply?
qa.a: It gave him room to admit he felt the same about his gym videos, so he didn't have to feel alone either.

grounding: A teenager hides doubts behind a polished online self, feels alone among many followers, and one real disclosure starts to change that.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10. Parveen.
Imran (15) came in to "ask about streams" and spent ten minutes on marks. Classmates see him as the funny one, and his short videos get big numbers. Near the end, looking at the floor, he said, "Everyone knows me and nobody knows me." He told me he deletes any post where he looks tired or unsure. I thanked him for telling me, said many students feel this and it isn't a weakness, and asked if there was one person he'd trust with one small true thing. He named his cousin Faiz. Plan: he will tell Faiz one honest thing this week. I'll check in with him at lunch on Wednesday, and we meet again on Friday.

qa.q: What did Imran say he deletes?
qa.a: Any post where he looks tired or unsure.

qa.q: What does Imran looking at the floor while saying "Everyone knows me and nobody knows me" suggest?
qa.a: He feels lonely behind his funny image and is nervous about admitting it, as if afraid of being judged.

qa.q: Why was asking Imran to share one small true thing with Faiz a good step?
qa.a: It keeps the risk small, so he can test whether honesty brings rejection or closeness, with the counsellor checking in along the way.

qa.q: How might Faiz be affected if Imran shares something honest?
qa.a: Faiz may feel trusted and closer to Imran, and might open up in return 🙂

grounding: A teenager who shows a polished, funny self feels unknown and alone, and a counsellor helps him take a first small step toward real disclosure.

passage:
Thursday, 10:40 pm
The class group was full of Samir's birthday pics tonight. I'm in six of them, laughing. Nobody would guess I spent half the party in the washroom because I felt like a fake.
I keep a version of me for them: chill, good at football, never stressed. The real one is scared of failing the maths re-test and thinks nobody would stay if they saw him.
But on the walk home Samir asked, "Bro, you okay? You went missing." And I said... actually, no. Told him about the re-test. He said he failed chemistry last term and hid it too!!
Didn't expect that. Feel lighter. Also weird. Going to sleep.
Kunal

qa.q: Where did Kunal spend half of Samir's party?
qa.a: In the washroom.

qa.q: Why did Kunal feel like a fake at the party?
qa.a: He was hiding his fear about the maths re-test behind a chill, never-stressed version of himself, and worried nobody would stay if they saw the real him.

qa.q: What choice on the walk home changed things for Kunal?
qa.a: When Samir asked, Kunal told the truth about the re-test instead of saying he was fine, and found he wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when Kunal went missing at the party?
qa.a: Samir noticed and seems to have been worried, and may have felt relieved to share the hidden chemistry result too.

grounding: A teenager who keeps a polished image feels fake and alone among friends until one honest disclosure brings unexpected closeness.

passage:
October. Parul skipped her Kathak class again to sit with Harish in the canteen. "You don't mind, na?" she asked. He shrugged. She told her friend Anu she'd come for Sunday lunch "next time."
December. Anu's messages sat unread. Parul realised she had laughed at Harish's jokes all month but couldn't remember her own last idea. In her hostel room the ankle bells hung dusty on a nail. She felt small, and oddly lonely beside someone she loved.
February. "Tuesdays and Thursdays are dance," Parul told Harish. "Sunday I'm with Anu." He frowned, then asked, "Fine. When's the recital?" That evening she practised until her feet ached, and for the first time in months she called him with news of her own.

qa.q: What hung dusty on a nail in Parul's hostel room in December?
qa.a: Her ankle bells.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling in December when she couldn't remember her own last idea?
qa.a: She felt small and oddly lonely, even beside someone she loved, as if she had lost part of herself.

qa.q: What choice in February changed things, and why did it help?
qa.a: Parul told Harish her dance days and her Sunday with Anu. Keeping her own time gave her news of her own to share, so she was close without disappearing.

qa.q: How might Harish see Parul's new schedule?
qa.a: At first he seems unsettled, since he frowns, but then he asks about her recital, so he may come to enjoy a partner with her own life.

grounding: A young woman in her first serious relationship drops her dance and friends, then reclaims them and finds closeness works better with her self intact.

passage: Sit, Dhruv. You asked why I look worried when you vanish with your girlfriend for weeks. Let me tell you about your Chacha, Manoj, at twenty. I did the opposite. I loved a girl in my B.Com class, Kiran, but I kept her at arm's length. I never told her Baba's shop was failing, never let her meet my friends, never let her see me upset. I thought a wall kept me safe. Once she said, "I feel like I'm dating your good side." She left after a year. Years later, with your Chachi, I tried something new. I showed her the messy parts, and I still kept my Sunday chess with my friends. Close, but still me. So don't vanish, and don't hide. Both cost me something.

qa.q: What did Kiran once say to Manoj?
qa.a: "I feel like I'm dating your good side."

qa.q: Why did Manoj keep Kiran at arm's length?
qa.a: He thought a wall kept him safe, so he was afraid of getting hurt if she saw troubles like Baba's failing shop.

qa.q: What did Manoj do differently with Chachi, and why did it work better?
qa.a: He showed her the messy parts while still keeping Sunday chess with his friends, so he was both close and still himself.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt in that relationship?
qa.a: She probably felt shut out and lonely, as if she only knew a polished version of him, which is why she left.

grounding: An uncle recalls keeping a partner at arm's length and later learning to be close while keeping his own friends and self.

passage: It was the week before semester exams, the hostel team's final was on Saturday, and Leena had asked Hrithik to help at her cousin's engagement that same evening. For two months he had said yes to everything she wanted. He had skipped practice four times, and Pankaj, his oldest friend, had stopped saving him a seat at dinner. Sitting on the hostel stairs with twelve percent battery, Hrithik typed "Of course I'll come" and stopped. He thought of Pankaj's face at the last match. He deleted it and wrote, "I'm playing the final at five, it matters to me. I'll come straight after, maybe by eight." The reply took ages. "Okay. A bit sad, but okay." Then he messaged Pankaj: "Still need a striker?"

qa.q: How many times had Hrithik skipped practice?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How was Hrithik feeling when he deleted "Of course I'll come"?
qa.a: He felt uneasy about how far he'd drifted from Pankaj and his team, and realised the final mattered to him too.

qa.q: What made Hrithik's reply to Leena a balanced choice?
qa.a: He kept his commitment to the team and still offered to come afterwards, staying close to Leena without giving up something that matters to him.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel on getting "Still need a striker?"
qa.a: Pankaj may feel glad to have an old friend back, though perhaps a little wary after two months of empty seats 🙂

grounding: A young man who has dropped his friends and sport for a new relationship chooses to stay close to his partner while keeping his own life.

passage: Rajni had eight hundred contacts and a phone that buzzed all day, yet most afternoons she ate lunch alone at her desk in the insurance office. On Friday she carried two cups of tea to the pantry, where Vishal was rinsing his lunchbox. They hadn't really spoken since she snapped at him in the client meeting. "I was rude," she said. "I'm sorry. I've had a rough month, and I took it out on you." Vishal dried his hands slowly. "It stung," he said. "But thanks." The silence was awkward. She stayed in it. "Would you want a Wednesday lunch? Just us, and maybe Ritu?" He took the tea. "Wednesdays work." Back at her desk, she muted three noisy group chats and set a reminder to call her college friend on Sunday.

qa.q: How many contacts did Rajni have?
qa.a: Eight hundred.

qa.q: Why did Rajni stay in the awkward silence instead of leaving?
qa.a: She wanted to repair the friendship for real and was willing to feel uncomfortable rather than escape it.

qa.q: Which choice after the pantry shows Rajni moving from a crowd to depth?
qa.a: She muted three noisy group chats and set a reminder to call her college friend, putting her energy into a few real people.

qa.q: What might Vishal feel when Rajni admits she was rude?
qa.a: He was hurt, as "It stung" shows, but her honest apology and mention of a rough month let him feel respected and willing to try again.

grounding: A lonely young woman with many contacts repairs a rift honestly and puts her time into a few close people.

passage:
Hi Tanvir,
It's been four months since your birthday, when I left early and then went silent after you said I only call when I need something. You were partly right, and it hurt, so I hid.
Here's the honest bit. Since I moved to Hyderabad my calendar is packed: office drinks, gym friends, three wedding groups. And I've never felt lonelier. Nobody here knows I've been struggling in the new role, because I keep everything light, and Ma tells everyone her daughter is thriving.
I don't want more people. I want the few who knew me before. So could we try a call every other Sunday? It'll be awkward at first. I'm fine with awkward.
And I'm sorry about your birthday.
Sudha

qa.q: What did Tanvir say that Sudha admits was partly right?
qa.a: That Sudha only calls when she needs something.

qa.q: What does "I'm fine with awkward" show about what Sudha wants?

qa.a: Realising she felt lonelier than ever because nobody around her knew she was struggling; that led her to reach for someone who knew her before.

passage: What changed for me this year, Gurleen? Honestly? I deleted nothing and left nothing. I just stopped counting. I, Kishore, had a thousand followers and four hundred numbers in my phone, and on my twenty-fifth birthday I sat in my rented room wishing one person would call for no reason. So I picked three: my brother, my school friend Salim and my old flatmate. I call each one on a fixed day, even for five minutes. The first calls were stiff; we'd talk scores and hang up. Then I told Salim I was scared of losing my job. He went quiet, then said his marriage was going through a hard time. We fought in August. I called the next week, said sorry, and it was awkward for three calls. It's still the best thing I have.

qa.q: Who are the three people Kishore picked?
qa.a: Kishore's brother, school friend Salim and old flatmate.

qa.q: What was Kishore wishing for on the twenty-fifth birthday, and what does it reveal?
qa.a: Kishore wished one person would call for no reason, which reveals deep loneliness despite hundreds of contacts.

qa.q: What choice after the August fight kept the friendship with Salim alive?
qa.a: Kishore called the next week to say sorry and put up with three awkward calls rather than letting the fight end things.

qa.q: What might Salim have felt when Kishore admitted being scared of losing the job?
qa.a: Salim may have felt trusted and safe enough to share his own hard time, so the honesty went both ways.

grounding: A young adult lonely among many contacts invests in three people through regular calls, honest talk about struggles and awkward repair after a fight.

passage: You want to know how Hrithik and I became friends? It took most of a year. When I, Pankaj, joined the site office, he was the engineer who ate alone in the jeep. Ask him about his weekend and he'd say, "Nothing much. What about the pour schedule?" He said no to the Diwali lunch, no to cricket, no to my cousin's wedding. I didn't push. I just started buying two cups of tea at five and leaving one on his dashboard. Some days he drank it, some days it went cold. Around March he walked with me to the gate. In June he mentioned, very quickly, that his father was ill back in Nagpur. I didn't ask more than he offered. Last week he invited me to his flat for dinner. That was his idea, not mine.

qa.q: What did Pankaj leave on Hrithik's dashboard?
qa.a: A cup of tea, bought at five.

qa.q: What might Hrithik's quick mention of his ill father suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: He was carrying a worry he didn't usually share; saying it quickly suggests he was starting to trust Pankaj but still felt guarded.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj's choice not to ask more matter?
qa.a: It let Hrithik keep control over what he shared, so trust kept growing until the dinner invitation came from him.

qa.q: What might the months of tea have been like for Hrithik?
qa.a: They were probably a steady, quiet sign that someone cared, letting him warm up at his own pace without being put on the spot.

grounding: A colleague keeps offering low-pressure company to a co-worker who deflects and declines, and trust builds slowly at that person's pace.

passage: I'm Preeti, and I teach Class 6 English. Jagdish joined our staff room in June to teach science. I can't tell you what was going on inside him; I can only say what I saw. He kept his lunchbox shut until the rest of us had left. When Sunita ma'am asked if he was married, he laughed and said, "Married to lab reports." He skipped the staff picnic and the farewell tea. I didn't know if he was shy, sad or just private. So every Friday I asked, "Walking to the bus stop? No pressure." He said no six Fridays in a row. On the seventh he said, "Okay, today." We mostly walked in silence. Now we walk every Friday, and last week he told me about his mother's village. I still don't know everything. I don't need to.

qa.q: What did Jagdish say when asked if he was married?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "Married to lab reports."

qa.q: How did Preeti feel about not knowing what was going on inside Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti felt unsure whether he was shy, sad or just private, so she kept offering the Friday walk with no pressure. She is content not to know everything.

qa.q: What choice did Preeti make after six refusals, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Preeti kept asking calmly each Friday without pushing or taking offence, so Jagdish could join when he was ready 🙂

qa.q: Why might Jagdish have kept his lunchbox shut until the others left?
qa.a: He may have wanted privacy or felt shy about questions; the passage leaves it open, just as Preeti does.

grounding: A colleague notices a new teacher who deflects questions and skips gatherings, and keeps offering easy company until he joins in his own time.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 9 writing project. Anirban.
Dolma (14) handed in her "People I Admire" piece a day late and asked to talk. She had written about both grandmothers. One lost her shop in a flood and still hums while making momos and waves at every neighbour. The other, she wrote, "counts old insults like beads." In our chat Dolma asked, very seriously, "How do you know which one you'll become?" I said I didn't know for certain, and asked what she'd noticed each of them doing every day. She thought for a long time and said, "One keeps letting go, I think." Next: I've suggested she interview both for the oral-history unit, and I'll check in with her afterwards.

qa.q: Who did Dolma write about in her piece?
qa.a: Both of her grandmothers.

qa.q: What was Dolma worried about when she asked, "How do you know which one you'll become?"
qa.a: She was worried she might end up like the grandmother who counts old insults, and unsure what decides which path a person takes.

qa.q: Why was Anirban's question about what each grandmother does every day a good response?
qa.a: It gave no lecture; it let Dolma notice for herself that daily habits, like letting go, seem to matter.

qa.q: How might the humming grandmother react if Dolma interviews her?
qa.a: She might be glad to be asked and share how she kept going after the flood, giving Dolma more to think about 🙂

grounding: A teenager compares a content grandmother with a bitter one and wonders which she will become, a question that stays with her.

Sunday, 9 pm
Family lunch at Dadu's today. Dadu laughed the whole time, told the burnt-kheer story for the hundredth time and let Arnab beat him at carrom. He's eighty and still waters his tulsi like it's a friend.
Then Nana came. Complained about the food, the traffic, his pension, and a cousin who "cheated him" in 1985. Nobody argued. Arnab rolled his eyes at me, his big sister.
Both are old. Both had hard lives, I think. Maa says Dadu lost his job twice. So why is one light and one heavy?
I don't want to be heavy. But I don't even know how you choose that. Or if you choose it at all.
Gopika

qa.a: Beat him at carrom.

qa.a: She wonders why one grandfather is light and one heavy though both had hard lives, and she worries about which one she might become.

qa.q: What small step could help Gopika explore her question?
qa.a: She could ask Dadu how he kept laughing after losing his job twice, and listen to Nana's story too, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Nana feel if he noticed Arnab rolling his eyes?
qa.a: He might feel dismissed and even more bitter, since nobody seems to really listen to him.

grounding: A teenager watches a cheerful grandfather and a bitter one at the same lunch and wonders which path she will take, without yet knowing how it is chosen.

passage: The power went off at nine, and Sumit sat on the roof of their house in the kasba with a torch and his exam notes, now copied out for the third time. Below, his mother Urmila was washing pots at the hand pump. He pictured himself at sixty, a clerk in the same block office, never having asked if he wanted it, never having told Amma he knew she had sold her earrings for his college fees. His chest went tight. For weeks the fear had made him copy his notes more neatly, as if a perfect page could save his life. Tonight he climbed down instead. "Amma," he said, holding the torch for her, "I know about the earrings." She stopped scrubbing. "I want to thank you. And I want to talk about what I actually want to do."

qa.q: How many times had Sumit copied out his exam notes?
qa.a: He had copied them out for the third time.

qa.q: Why did Sumit's chest go tight on the roof?
qa.a: He was scared of a life full of regret: a job he never questioned and never telling Amma he knew about the earrings.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Sumit that night, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He climbed down to speak to Amma instead of copying notes more neatly; acting honestly now eased the fear in a way perfect pages couldn't.

qa.q: What might Urmila feel when she stops scrubbing?
qa.a: She may be surprised and moved that her son knew about the earrings, and a little nervous about what he wants to discuss.

grounding: A student imagines himself at sixty with a safe job never questioned and thanks left unsaid, and turns from perfectionism to speaking honestly to his mother.

subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
passage: On the crowded minibus home through Addis Ababa, Esther watched an old man across the aisle staring out of the window, a folder of papers on his knees. Suddenly she pictured herself at sixty on this same route, still in the accounting job her uncle had arranged, never having asked whether she even liked numbers, never having told her father, Abebe, that she had forgiven him for the years he worked abroad. Her hands went cold. That week she had rewritten her internship essay eleven times, as if one perfect paragraph could promise a good life. At home, her father was frying onions. Esther put her bag down. "Aba, can I tell you something I've never said?" He turned down the flame and pulled out a chair.

qa.q: How many times had Esther rewritten her internship essay?
qa.a: Eleven times that week.

qa.q: What made Esther's hands go cold on the minibus?
qa.a: She imagined herself at sixty with regrets, an unquestioned job and words never said to her father, and the fear of that life gripped her.

qa.q: What choice did Esther make at home, and how is it different from rewriting the essay?
qa.a: She chose to tell her father something she had never said. Instead of chasing perfection, she acted honestly now on the regret she feared.

qa.q: What might Abebe be feeling when he turns down the flame and pulls out a chair?
qa.a: He seems to sense something important and wants to listen fully, though he may be a little nervous about what his daughter will say.

grounding: A student imagines being sixty with an unquestioned job and unsaid words to her father, and chooses honest speech over perfect essays.
